name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
title: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
answer: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool to ask the kinds of questions a historian would ask while students read letters, speeches, photographs, and government records. The tool prompts students to consider who made a source, when, why, what it omits, and who might see it differently, but it does not tell them what the source means. This matters because students build historical reading skills over years, and the AI supports their own interpretation rather than replacing it.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Primary sources are the raw material of history, and reading them well is a skill that develops over years. Many archives and libraries, including the Library of Congress and state archives, make large collections available at no cost. The problem this idea solves is that students need help learning how to question a source without having an AI tool do the interpreting for them. A school configured tool can act as a coach by asking the questions a historian would ask, such as who created the document and what the author was trying to accomplish. The student answers and receives follow up questions, while the meaning of the source remains the student's work to determine.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher can set up a hint only tool, as described in Chapter 7, to help students plan an essay from a set of documents without writing the essay for them. The tool might ask which documents support the student's argument and which complicate it, leaving the reading, reasoning, and writing to the student. Document based questions fit this approach because they require students to work with multiple sources and build an argument. The supplied text does not give grade bands, so the practice is described generally rather than by grade level. Teachers choose the sources themselves, and students use the coach to read real sources from archives, library databases, or trusted collections.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text does not provide a research study, figure, finding, or evidence label for this idea. It describes a practice: an AI coach that asks historian style questions, a hint only tool from Chapter 7, and document based questions. It also notes that the Library of Congress and many state archives offer large collections of primary sources free of charge, which is a statement about available resources rather than research evidence. On the text as given, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. AI tools can suggest documents, but they sometimes describe documents that do not exist or misquote real ones, so every source students use should come from an archive, a library database, or a trusted collection. Teachers should choose the sources themselves rather than relying on AI suggestions. The coach must not tell students what a source means, and the student keeps the work of reading, reasoning, and writing. The decisions about which sources to use, how to set up the hint only tool, and how to guide interpretation stay with the teacher and the student.
